title: A Rainforest Near the South Pole
place: Seabed near Pine Island and Thwaites glaciers, West Antarctica
text: A sediment core drilled into the seabed of West Antarctica held a dense network of fossil roots, plus countless grains of pollen and spores. They come from a 90-million-year-old temperate rainforest, like those of New Zealand today, growing within 900 km of the South Pole. Summers averaged about 19 degrees Celsius, and swamp and river water reached up to 20 degrees.

source.name: Imperial College London: Traces of ancient rainforest in Antarctica point to a warmer prehistoric world

title: Ice Age Hunters at the Arctic Circle
place: Mamontovaya Kurya, Usa River, Komi Republic, Russia
text: At Mamontovaya Kurya, in the European part of the Russian Arctic, people were living nearly 40,000 years ago, during the last ice age. Russian and Norwegian archaeologists dug up hundreds of animal bones, stone tools, and a mammoth tusk that appears to have been cut by those very tools. Their report appeared in the journal Nature in 2001.

source.name: Scientific American: Humans Lived North of the Arctic Circle During Last Ice Age

title: The Oldest Art of the Arctic
place: Yana RHS, Yana River, Sakha Republic (Yakutia), Russia
text: The Yana site in Arctic Siberia, dated to about 28,000 years ago, holds the earliest art ever excavated in the Arctic zone. Its people made decorated beads, pendants and needles, plus shallow dishes and human-like designs carved on mammoth tusks. Archaeologists see echoes of these images in the hunting and shamanic art of the Indigenous Yukaghir people recorded in the early 1900s.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge Core): Oldest art of the Eurasian Arctic: personal ornaments and symbolic objects from Yana RHS, Arctic Siberia

title: Siberian Roots on the Kola Peninsula
place: Bolshoy Oleni Ostrov, Murmansk Region, Russia
text: About 3,500 years ago, people were buried at Bolshoy Oleni Ostrov on the Kola Peninsula, a region where Saami live today. Their DNA revealed that about half their ancestry came from Siberia, the earliest evidence of Siberian ancestry in Fennoscandia. Among Europeans today, the Saami carry the largest share of this ancient Siberian ancestry.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Ancient Fennoscandian genomes reveal origin and spread of Siberian ancestry in Europe

source2.name: Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History: First ancient DNA from mainland Finland

title: A Town of Whalebone Houses
place: Ipiutak site, Tikigaq (Point Hope), North Slope, Alaska, USA
text: On the Tikigaq spit, which juts into the Chukchi Sea, over 500 house ruins line the old beach ridges, making Ipiutak one of the largest early village sites in Arctic Alaska. The houses were surrounded by big whale and walrus bones. Ipiutak communities, famous for fine carving in ivory, wood, bone and stone, reached their peak population between AD 650 and 870.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service: Ipiutak Site

title: The Dorset, or Tuniit, Appear
text: Around 2,800 years ago, the Dorset Palaeo-Inuit emerged in the Arctic, named by archaeologist Diamond Jenness after Kinngait, then called Cape Dorset. They built sunken-floor houses for winter and lit and heated their world with soapstone lamps, yet show little sign of dogsleds or bows. Inuit oral histories remember an earlier people, the Tuniit, whom many consider the same group.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Dorset Culture (Patrick Jolicoeur)

title: The Bone Man of Ust-Polui
place: Ust-Polui, Salekhard, Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, Russia
text: Inside today's city of Salekhard lies Ust-Polui, a sanctuary used around 100 BCE to 100 CE. Digs in the 1930s found about 7,000 objects, 1,500 of them finely made from bone. In 2009 archaeologists uncovered a 7.3 cm figure of a seated man hugging his knees, carved from deer antler with an iron knife. Permafrost even preserved decorated birch-bark objects.

source.name: SCIENCE First Hand (Siberian Branch, Russian Academy of Sciences): The Land of Ancestors. The Bone Man and Other Secrets of the Ancient Sanctuary

source2.name: Archaeology, Ethnology and Anthropology of Eurasia: Decorated Birch-Bark Artifacts from the Ust-Polui Sanctuary (100 BC to 100 AD)

title: Rome's Smog, Frozen in Greenland
text: Lead from Roman silver mining and smelting drifted all the way to Greenland and was locked in its ice. Scientists measuring about 1,300 feet of ice found lead pollution peaked in the first century CE, then dropped dramatically around the year 165, likely because of the Antonine Plague. It stayed low for more than 500 years.

source.name: Archaeology magazine (Archaeological Institute of America): Ice Core Study Tracks Roman Lead Levels

source2.name: PNAS (University of Copenhagen research portal): Lead pollution recorded in Greenland ice indicates European emissions tracked plagues, wars, and imperial expansion during antiquity

title: Polynesians in the Subantarctic
place: Sandy Bay, Enderby Island, Auckland Islands, New Zealand
text: Radiocarbon dates show that a group of Polynesians and their dogs lived on windswept Enderby Island for at least one summer in the 1200s or 1300s. Food remains reveal they ate Hooker's sea lions, fur seals, sooty shearwaters, albatrosses and penguins. Their camp at Sandy Bay is the southernmost known site of prehistoric Polynesian voyaging.

source.name: New Zealand Department of Conservation: Enderby Island Māori occupation

title: Kerguelen Thinks He Found a Continent
place: Kerguelen Islands, French Southern and Antarctic Lands
text: Sailing south from Mauritius with the ships Fortune and Gros Ventre, Breton officer Yves-Joseph de Kerguelen reached an island in the southern Indian Ocean in February 1772, and it was claimed for France. Fog split the ships, and Kerguelen returned to France claiming he had found the great southern land. In truth the island was icy and inhospitable; Cook later named it after him.

source.name: Western Australian Museum: De Kerguelen and de Saint Aloüarn 1771–1772

title: What Inuit Saw of Franklin's Men
place: Near O'Reilly Island, Adelaide Peninsula, Nunavut, Canada
text: Franklin's ships Erebus and Terror were trapped in ice in 1846, and in April 1848 the 105 surviving crew abandoned them. Inuit later said about 40 white men were seen heading south along King William Island. An Inuk named Inukpujijuk marked a wreck's location on explorer Charles Francis Hall's chart, and in 2014 searchers found HMS Erebus close to that spot.

source.name: Parks Canada: Wrecks of HMS Erebus and HMS Terror National Historic Site, Inuit traditional knowledge

title: The First International Polar Year
text: Austro-Hungarian naval officer Karl Weyprecht argued that big results needed many expeditions observing at the same time. The result was the first International Polar Year, 1882–1883, with 12 camps. Near Barrow, Ray's team adapted to local ways, once travelling with local people by dog sled to the Prudhoe Bay area; all came home healthy. Far north on Ellesmere Island, Greely's party of 25 shrank to seven.

source.name: University of Alaska Fairbanks Geophysical Institute, Alaska Science Forum: First International Polar Year was edgy affair (Ned Rozell)

title: An Ice Shelf Shatters in a Month
place: Larsen B Ice Shelf, Antarctic Peninsula, Antarctica
text: In the southern summer of 2002, almost the entire Larsen B Ice Shelf, about 3,250 square kilometres, splintered and collapsed in just over a month. A run of warm summers ended in an exceptionally warm one, and melt ponds on the surface acted like wedges. Freed from the shelf, the glaciers behind it sped up, by about 300 percent on average.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: World of Change: Collapse of the Larsen-B Ice Shelf
